chapters.label: Intro
chapters.text: Happy Tuesday. The Spurs won, a tech CEO got his job back like nothing happened, and FIFA's president has apparently been living on a plane. Let's get into it.

chapters.label: 🏆 My Teams
chapters.text: Start with the good stuff: the Spurs beat the Kings 123 to 107 and they're 15 and 3. Stephon Castle did a bit of everything, 28 points, 8 rebounds and 11 assists. That's a point guard stat line with a scorer's bonus. Fifteen and 3 is the kind of record you check twice. Sacramento never really got a say.

chapters.label: 🏛️ Politics
chapters.text: Jensen Huang is back as CEO of Nvidia, the chip giant at the center of the AI boom. He resigned less than two weeks ago after reports of extramarital affairs, one of them with an alleged Chinese spy. The board reinstated him Monday, and President Trump took some credit. Congress was not charmed. A House Intelligence spokesperson said the reinstatement quote changes nothing, and Huang is still due for a transcribed interview on December 1 with three House panels, including the Select Committee on China. Nvidia's general counsel appears December 2, and Huang is due before Senate Banking on December 3. So the man who got fired over his pillow talk now gets to explain it to people with subpoena power and no sense of humor. National security is the actual concern here, and chips are the thing China wants most.

chapters.label: 🇺🇸 U.S.
chapters.text: Jose Castillo is an American citizen, and he says he felt useless. On Saturday, masked ICE agents arrested his wife, Sofia Hernandez Mejia, and his father-in-law, Ricardo Larrondo Mendoza, inside a jetway at Seattle-Tacoma airport. Video of it went viral, with her crying out that she has a valid work permit and bystanders demanding answers. The Department of Homeland Security says both are Mexican nationals who overstayed their visas, and that agents were targeting the father-in-law when other passengers got in the way. It also accuses her of assault, saying she threw hot coffee on officers. Castillo says she did nothing, that she was being shoved, and that when people come at you like that, quote, obviously coffee's going to be spilled. DHS has said she will face charges.

chapters.label: 🏈 Sports
chapters.text: Thirty-nine private jet flights in a hundred and fifteen days. That's FIFA president Gianni Infantino since the news broke on July 28 that he wanted to sell off a stake in the World Cup, according to BBC Sport. He hit 32 countries, flew more than 102,000 miles and spent nearly nine days in the air. Last year he visited 18 countries over the same stretch. FIFA says he has a duty to keep relationships healthy with its 211 member associations. Critics call it a campaign tour ahead of his re-election vote next March, and a former head of FIFA's governance committee says it's exactly that. The loophole is that FIFA has no campaign funding rules, so it's all just official business. And it seems to be working, since he's now the favorite.

chapters.label: 🏈 Sports
chapters.text: Florida State got its man. Georgia defensive coordinator Glenn Schumann agreed to a five-year deal to replace Mike Norvell, who was fired after a 3 and 5 start. Schumann has six national titles from his time at Alabama and Georgia, and Georgia is ranked number one in the playoff rankings. He'll stay put through the postseason, so he's basically coaching a title run with one eye on a moving truck. The new athletic director, Jeff Purinton, worked with him under Nick Saban at Alabama. Schumann's grandfather even coached on Florida State's very first team in 1947, so this is a homecoming of sorts.

chapters.label: 🏈 Sports
chapters.text: Micah Parsons is expected to make his season debut Wednesday night for the Packers against the Rams. Sources say he got final clearance Monday from Dr. Neal ElAttrache, the surgeon who fixed the knee he wrecked in Week 15 last year, when he tore both his ACL and his meniscus against Denver. That's 347 days between snaps. The Packers are 6 and 4 and somehow in last place in the NFC North, where the Bears, Lions and Vikings are all 7 and 2. Parsons said he understands what this game means for the playoffs. Green Bay needs a pass rusher who can wreck a game, and now it has one.

chapters.label: 🎬 Culture & Entertainment
chapters.text: A Don Toliver concert at Co-op Live in Manchester ended in an evacuation on Sunday night. Around 10 p.m., an unknown substance was released into the crowd. Fans described a horrible smell, screaming and people struggling to breathe. About 12,000 people were evacuated, one woman went to hospital and 88 others were checked by paramedics for eye and respiratory symptoms. Police declared a major incident and first thought it was tear gas. No arrests yet, and detectives are still working out what the substance was and whether a crime was committed. Some fans are also complaining about the lack of searches at the door, which is a question the venue is going to have to answer.

chapters.label: 🎬 Culture & Entertainment
chapters.text: The first ever Children's Booker Prize has a shortlist: eight books, aimed at kids eight to twelve, with fifty thousand pounds on the line. Five novels, two graphic novels and an illustrated short story collection. Eoin Colfer, of Artemis Fowl fame, is in there. The fun part is the judges: four kids picked from more than 4,000 entrants, including twelve-year-old Ibrahim from Hampshire, who says being a judge on his CV will take him a long way. Chair Frank Cottrell-Boyce is blunt about it: if the children don't love a book, it won't win. Ibrahim won't reveal his favorite, but he did say his mum confiscated one of the shortlisted books because he couldn't stop reading it and it was giving him a headache. That's the best blurb I've heard all year.

chapters.label: ⚡ Quick hits
chapters.text: Quick hits. The Pentagon put out an unusually blunt fact sheet saying Canada has fallen short as a defense partner, citing its military spending and its second look at buying American F-35 fighter jets. Three Russian cruise missiles landed in rural southeastern Poland on Friday, and no one was hurt. Poland's prime minister called it an intentional provocation, and NATO's Mark Rutte is trying to calm eastern members. Ousted Bangladeshi leader Sheikh Hasina says she'll return from exile in India on December 16, though she's been sentenced to death in absentia and is expected to be arrested on arrival. Virginia and Oregon became the first states to sue SpaceX, which now owns xAI, claiming Grok still generates sexual images of real people, including children. And the COP31 climate talks collapsed after oil producers blocked any mention of phasing out fossil fuels.

chapters.label: Wrapping up
chapters.text: That's your Tuesday. Go Spurs, and may your boss never need a congressional hearing to explain his weekend. Talk tomorrow.
